newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britsh Airways seeks 5,000 job losses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britsh Airways seeks 5,000 job losses.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Wednesday it wanted to shed 5,000 of its 49,000 British staff to make way for new recruits with different skills as part of a major three-year restructuring campaign.

The jobs plan was unveiled by chief executive Robert Ayling to 300 senior managers as part of the airline's ambitious "Step Change" efficiency drive which aims to lop one billion pounds ($1.56 billion) from its annual cost base by 2000.
Promising that no jobs in the airline would unaffected by the plans, he said some would be outsourced, some relocated and some ended.
BA said it was considering whether it was cheaper to contract out many of its ancillary operations in Britain, including check-in, baggage loading, cargo handling and some financial services.

"Some activities could be sold or subcontracted if they can be done better or more cheaply externally, with employees involved being offered jobs with the new owner, redeployed within the airline with retraining, or taking voluntary severance or early retirement," the airline said in a statement.

BA wants around 5,000 staff to take voluntary severance or early retirement over the next 18 months and Ayling said this was "to create room for a huge programme of redeployment and retraining" which would also see BA taking on about 5,000 new staff over the next three years.
Ayling said he could not rule out compulsory redundancies "but I don't expect that is going to be a problem here." He was due to present the plans to the main staff unions on Wednesday evening.

"There is no reason why their response should be anything other than positive," he told a news conference. "I do not expect wholesale job losses. Jobs will also be created, and jobs secured. We will grow and we will improve. I am committed to a strategy of investment and improved profitability."
The Transport and General Workers Union, which represents many of BA's cabin crew and ground service staff, declined to comment ahead of the meeting.

BA ranks as the biggest international carrier and one of the most profitable airlines in the world, but Ayling said it needed to improve services and cut costs if it was to fight off new competition and offset falls in average fare levels and the rising cost of handling more traffic.

"The competition is getting better and more efficient. Our customers expect more but our cost of providing a seat has risen faster than the price customers pay in a highly-competitive marketplace," he said.

Under the Step Change programme managers and staff have been given the task of identifying radical ways of becoming more efficient to cut the airline's annual cost base by one billion pounds over the next three years.

Ayling said this would probably mean contracting out some operations, opening up the prospect of BA imitating the low cost airlines pioneered by Southwest in the U.S. which buy in many of their ancillary services.

"What we want to do is improve customer service, reduce the cost of producing the services, to make our assets work better and not to be too worried about ownership if that's something which is going to stand in our way," he said.

"We will be making sure that wherever possible services provided within the company are at competitive rates...If that can't be achieved then we will buy in the services rather than provide them from within the company." ($1=.6415 Pound)
